overview: Welsh (Cymraeg) is a Celtic language of the Brythonic branch, spoken in Wales and documented from the sixth century onward. The Middle Welsh period (c. 1100–1400) produced the Mabinogion and court poetry of the Gogynfeirdd; Modern Literary Welsh (fifteenth century to present) encompasses the cynghanedd masters Dafydd ap Gwilym and Tudur Aled, as well as twentieth-century poets and prose writers such as Saunders Lewis, Kate Roberts, and R. S. Thomas. Study of Welsh offers access to a continuous literary tradition of thirteen centuries, a unique prosodic system, and a living minority language with constitutional status in the United Kingdom.

alphabet.name: a
alphabet.approximation: like a in father (short or long)
alphabet.notes: Circumflex indicates length: â [aː].

alphabet.name: ec
alphabet.notes: Never soft as in city. Before all vowels = [k].

alphabet.name: èch
alphabet.approximation: like ch in Scottish loch or German Bach
alphabet.notes: Digraph counted as single letter. Voiceless velar fricative.

alphabet.name: èdd
alphabet.approximation: like th in this or breathe
alphabet.notes: Digraph counted as single letter. Voiced dental fricative.

alphabet.name: e
alphabet.approximation: like e in bet (short) or é in café (long)
alphabet.notes: Circumflex indicates length: ê [eː].

alphabet.name: èff
alphabet.notes: Single f is always [v]. Lenition of b and m.

alphabet.name: èff
alphabet.notes: Digraph counted as single letter. Voiceless labiodental fricative.

alphabet.name: èg
alphabet.notes: Never soft as in gem. Before all vowels = [ɡ].

alphabet.name: èng
alphabet.notes: Digraph counted as single letter. Velar nasal. Also the nasal mutation of c.

alphabet.name: hâ
alphabet.notes: Occurs initially in aspirate mutation and in borrowings.

alphabet.name: i
alphabet.approximation: like i in sit (short) or ee in see (long)
alphabet.notes: Circumflex indicates length: î [iː]. Semivowel [j] before vowels.

alphabet.name: jot
alphabet.notes: Found only in borrowings from English (e.g., jins, jam).

alphabet.name: èll
alphabet.approximation: voiceless l; put tongue in position for l and blow
alphabet.notes: Digraph counted as single letter. Voiceless alveolar lateral fricative. No English equivalent.

alphabet.name: o
alphabet.approximation: like o in got (short) or aw in saw (long)
alphabet.notes: Circumflex indicates length: ô [oː].

alphabet.name: ffi
alphabet.notes: Digraph counted as single letter. Aspirate mutation of p.

alphabet.name: èr
alphabet.approximation: trilled r, as in Spanish perro
alphabet.notes: Alveolar trill or tap. Always pronounced, never silent.

alphabet.name: rhi
alphabet.approximation: voiceless r; say r while whispering
alphabet.notes: Digraph counted as single letter. Voiceless alveolar trill. Aspirate mutation of r.

alphabet.name: ès
alphabet.notes: Always voiceless [s], never [z].

alphabet.name: thèta
alphabet.approximation: like th in thing or thin
alphabet.notes: Digraph counted as single letter. Voiceless dental fricative. Aspirate mutation of t.

alphabet.name: u
alphabet.approximation: like i in sit (South) or a neutral vowel (North)
alphabet.notes: Regional variation. Circumflex indicates length: û. Middle Welsh distinguished u from i.

alphabet.name: w
alphabet.approximation: like oo in book (short) or oo in food (long)
alphabet.notes: Full vowel, not semivowel. Circumflex indicates length: ŵ [uː]. Also semivowel [w] before vowels.

alphabet.name: y
alphabet.approximation: like a in about (obscure) or i in sit (clear)
alphabet.notes: Full vowel. Two values: obscure [ə] in non-final syllables; clear [ɨ/ɪ] in final syllables and monosyllables. Circumflex indicates length: ŷ.

pronunciation_notes: The digraphs ch, dd, ff, ng, ll, ph, rh, th count as single letters and occupy separate dictionary positions.
Welsh is phonetic: words are pronounced as spelled. Stress falls on the penultimate (next-to-last) syllable in native words.
The letters w and y are vowels with full syllabic status, not glides. W = [ʊ/uː]; y has two values (obscure [ə] and clear [ɨ/ɪ]).
Ll [ɬ] has no English equivalent; place the tongue as for l and blow air voicelessly around the sides of the tongue.
Initial consonants undergo mutation (lenition, nasalization, aspiration, or mixed) depending on grammatical context. The same word may begin with different consonants.
R is always trilled; rh is the voiceless trill. Double consonants are not lengthened; they represent single sounds (ff = [f], not [ff]).

grammar.noun_system: Welsh nouns have no case inflection. Gender is grammatical (masculine or feminine) and determines the form of the definite article (y, yr, 'r) and triggers soft mutation of feminine singular nouns after the article. Number is marked by suffixes (plurals in -au, -iau, -oedd, -on, -i, -ydd) or by internal vowel change (ablaut); some nouns are collective with singulative suffixes. Middle Welsh preserved vestigial dative forms in prepositions but lacked a full case system even then.
grammar.declensions: Welsh has no declensional paradigm in the classical sense. Nouns are marked for number (singular/plural) and gender (masculine/feminine), but not for case. The following illustrates the typical plural formation patterns, which must be learned for each noun: **Masculine noun**: *bachgen* 'boy' (sg.) → *bechgyn* (pl.) by vowel change; **Feminine noun**: *cath* 'cat' (sg.) → *cathod* (pl.) by suffix -od. The definite article triggers soft mutation of feminine singular nouns: *cath* → *y gath* 'the cat'; masculine nouns remain unmutated: *bachgen* → *y bachgen* 'the boy'. Genitive relationships are expressed by simple juxtaposition (head noun + possessor): *tŷ'r dyn* 'the man's house' (house-the man), *pen y ci* 'the dog's head' (head the dog).
grammar.verb_system: Welsh has two verb systems: the periphrastic (analytic) and the synthetic (inflected). The periphrastic system dominates spoken and most written Welsh, using the auxiliary *bod* 'to be' plus the verbal noun: *mae e'n mynd* 'he goes/is going' (is he in going). The synthetic system survives in formal literary registers and consists of personal endings on the verb stem, marking person, number, tense, and mood. The tenses of the synthetic conjugation include present, imperfect, preterite (past), pluperfect, future, conditional, and subjunctive. Middle Welsh used the synthetic system extensively; Modern Welsh largely restricts it to *bod* itself and to literary style.

conjugations.name: bod 'to be' (irregular, periphrastic present/future)
conjugations.description: The verb bod is irregular and suppletive. The present tense uses forms from multiple roots (bod-, oes-, mae-, yw-). The periphrastic present with yn + verbal noun is the normal construction for other verbs. Future forms (byddaf, etc.) also serve as habitual present in some dialects.

conjugations.name: canu 'to sing' (regular verb, synthetic forms)
conjugations.description: Regular verbs in the synthetic conjugation take personal endings on the stem. The present tense is rare in Modern Welsh outside literary contexts; the preterite (past) is more common. The imperfect is marked by the infix -e- and personal endings. Middle Welsh used these forms routinely; Modern Literary Welsh preserves them in formal writing.

conjugations.name: mynd 'to go' (irregular verb, synthetic forms)
conjugations.description: Mynd is irregular with suppletive stems: â- (present), aeth- (preterite), and ai- (imperfect from older eid-). The present tense forms are literary. Periphrastic construction: mae e'n mynd 'he goes, he is going'. The preterite is used in both literary and colloquial registers.

reading_list: William Morgan's 1588 Bible (the foundational text of modern literary Welsh; public domain; by far the most accessible long-form Welsh prose available)
Aneirin, Y Gododdin (arguably the oldest surviving poetry from Britain; the largest hole in the original list, given Taliesin was already included)

Selections from the Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi), Middle Welsh prose, c. 1050–1120, ed. Ifor Williams (1930) or trans. Sioned Davies (2007) for beginners with facing translation.
Culhwch ac Olwen (the earliest Arthurian prose tale; in the Mabinogion but outside the Four Branches), plus Breuddwyd Macsen and the Three Romances (Owain, Peredur, Geraint)
Canu Llywarch Hen and Canu Heledd (the saga englynion — three- or four-line stanzas in a strict metre; the direct Welsh counterpart to the Old English elegies)
Cyfraith Hywel Dda (the medieval Welsh law texts; unusual and largely unavailable elsewhere in translation)
Selections from Dafydd ap Gwilym (fl. 1340–1370), cywyddau in cynghanedd, ed. Thomas Parry (1952). Begin with 'Y Gwynt' (The Wind) and 'Trafferth mewn Tafarn' (Trouble in a Tavern).
The cywyddwyr: Iolo Goch, Guto'r Glyn, Dafydd Nanmor (14th-15th c. poets working in the cywydd metre alongside Dafydd ap Gwilym)
Gruffudd ab yr Ynad Coch, elegy for Llywelyn (1282) — one of the great medieval Welsh poems
Ellis Wynne, Gweledigaethau y Bardd Cwsc (Visions of the Sleeping Bard), 1703, baroque allegory, accessible early Modern Welsh prose.
Ann Griffiths, hymns (d. 1805); Hen Benillion, the anonymous folk stanzas
T. Gwynn Jones, 'Ymadawiad Arthur' (The Passing of Arthur), awdl (ode) in cynghanedd, 1902, one of the great Victorian-era strict-meter poems.
Daniel Owen, Rhys Lewis (d. 1895, public domain) — the first major Welsh novel
The Book of Taliesin (Llyfr Taliesin), sixth–tenth century poems in archaic Welsh, advanced Old and Middle Welsh, ed. Marged Haycock (2007, bilingual).
The Black Book of Carmarthen (Llyfr Du Caerfyrddin), c. 1250, oldest surviving manuscript of Welsh poetry, archaic orthography, ed. A. O. H. Jarman (1982).
Medieval Welsh court poetry (Beirdd y Tywysogion, Poets of the Princes), twelfth–thirteenth century, ed. R. Geraint Gruffydd et al., in cynghanedd, historical and panegyric.

REMOVED: R.S. Thomas (d. 2000, in copyright until 2070) — and separately, he wrote his poetry in English, not Welsh, so he does not belong on a Welsh-language reader shelf regardless of copyright status. T. Gwynn Jones (d. 1949) remains — clear in life+70 territories. Because modern Welsh is almost entirely closed off by these copyright walls, the pre-1900 additions above (Morgan's Bible, Aneirin, the medieval law texts, Daniel Owen) carry more relative weight on this shelf than on any other language's list.
